source.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
source.authors: Minyoung Huh; Brian Cheung; Tongzhou Wang; Phillip Isola

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies representational alignment and convergence, not held-out loss scaling laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It discusses scaling in relation to representation convergence and cites scaling-law work, but does not test or rely on the claim as a tool.
record.gate_note: The paper reports relationships between representation alignment, language-modeling score, caption density, and downstream task performance. These are not tests of the claim versions: in particular, the downstream results relate performance to alignment rather than to scale or pretraining loss, and the paper does not fit or test loss-scaling laws. Scaling-law statements attributed to prior work are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures representational alignment between vision and language models and its correlation with language-modeling score and downstream tasks. It fits no loss power law, makes no extrapolation, does no compute-allocation or shape analysis, and does not relate downstream performance to scale or pretraining loss as a predictive law. Scaling-law work (Hestness 2017, Kaplan 2020) is only cited in passing, e.g. that methods scale with different efficiency. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses' because the scaling-law claim itself is not argued about.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that representations across architectures, objectives and modalities are converging toward a shared statistical model of reality (a PMI-like kernel), driven by scale, task generality and simplicity bias. They acknowledge limits: alignment is incomplete (about 0.16), depends on the metric, and may fail for modalities with different information or for special-purpose systems.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures representation alignment and downstream-task associations rather than evaluating loss-scaling fits or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment trends vary with the alignment metric and its hyperparameters; the authors also report differences by vision-model training task. Prompted language-model representations showed similar trends to average pooling but slightly lower alignment scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Better language-modeling score (1−bits-per-byte) goes with higher mutual-kNN alignment to vision models on WIT, but alignment peaks around 0.16 of a maximum of 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal representational alignment increases with model competence and scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Alignment to DINOv2 tracks Hellaswag (linear) and GSM8K (emergence-like) performance across about 20 LLMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-model alignment with vision representations correlates with downstream language-task performance.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The results do not measure held-out loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. The reported alignment and downstream relationships are largely presented as trends in figures; the paper notes that the cross-modal alignment score reaches only 0.16 on a metric whose maximum is 1, and that alignment depends on the metric and task setting.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Results about caption density, color cooccurrence, and vision-model alignment were omitted because they do not measure a version of the claim or add a distinct finding about its subject.

untested.parts: All of it: no held-out loss power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it: no extrapolation from small runs.
All of it: no compute-optimal allocation.
All of it: no depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
All of it: vision models are measured for alignment, not for loss power laws.
All of it: downstream scores are plotted against alignment, not against scale or pretraining loss.
All of it: no fitted exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. Kaplan et al. is cited once, for differing scaling efficiency. The study is not one of the claim's original sources, and no verdicts are given.

Extrapolation of losses from smaller to larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Loss differences among architectures at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling across modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance predictability from model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: language-model suite and vision-model suite
rows.size_stated: multiple scales; individual sizes not stated in the text result
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-modal representation alignment alongside language-modeling score.

conditions.value: WIT for alignment; 4M OpenWebText tokens for language-modeling performance

rows.measure: Relationship between language-modeling score (1 − bits-per-byte) and language-vision alignment
rows.value: The authors report that better language-modeling performance tends to accompany greater alignment with vision models.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result across the plotted language- and vision-model suite; this is an alignment relationship, not a fitted loss-scaling law.
rows.check: The measure is alignment versus 1−bits-per-byte, not loss versus scale, so it cannot show any version's effect. The 'observed' state refers to the alignment trend, not to the claim. It belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: language-model suite and DINOv2
rows.size_stated: multiple model sizes; individual sizes not stated in the text result
rows.operation_detail: Compared language-model alignment to DINOv2 with downstream task performance.
rows.measure: Downstream task performance in relation to alignment with vision
rows.value: The authors report a linear relationship: models with greater alignment also show better Hellaswag performance.
rows.note: The stated relationship is with alignment; model size is shown by marker radius and language-modeling score by color, not used as the reported predictor.
rows.check: The predictor is alignment to DINOv2, not scale or pretraining loss, so the row cannot bear on V6. Model size and LM score are only encoded as marker size and colour, with no fitted relation.
